title: Wave — Campus Community App
tagline: One app for campus life: events, carpools, housing, deals, tutoring, internships, and chat.
summary: A campus community app for students and student associations — events with bookings and comments, carpooling, housing, deals, tutoring with in-app purchases, internships, stories, and realtime chat. Expo React Native frontend, TypeScript/Express API over PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with a Redis-backed push pipeline and a Lydia payment integration.

caseStudy.problem:
Campus life is scattered: event announcements live in Instagram stories, carpool rides in WhatsApp groups, housing offers in class chats, and tutoring deals in corridor posters. Students juggle half a dozen channels, student associations have no unified way to reach members, and nothing records who booked what or who reported what. A student association needs one channel: post an event, take bookings, moderate comments, collect ride offers and housing listings, sell tutoring sessions, and reach members with push notifications.

Wave was built as that channel: a single mobile app where students and associations each have a real account, and every transaction — an event booking, a carpool seat, a tutoring purchase — is a first-class API object, not a message in a group.
requirements: Separate student and association accounts with JWT auth
Events with bookings, comments, and association-owned moderation
Marketplace modules: carpooling, housing, deals, tutoring, and internships
Tutoring sessions purchasable in-app with a real payment provider
Realtime conversations between students and associations
Push notifications delivered through Expo and Firebase Cloud Messaging
Stories and notifications so associations can broadcast to members
caseStudy.solution:
A TypeScript/Express monolith is the whole product surface — about thirty route modules covering auth, events, carpooling, housing, deals, tutoring, internships, conversations, stories, reports, and payments — served to an Expo React Native app and backed by two data stores: PostgreSQL (Sequelize) for the social core and MongoDB (Mongoose) for the conversation and marketplace collections. Redis runs a BullMQ push pipeline whose worker delivers to Expo/FCM with receipt reconciliation, Socket.IO and Pusher carry realtime chat, and payments go through a Lydia provider bound behind a dependency-injection token so controllers never name the provider.

The app in the store is the iOS and Android surface; the API in the repo is the source of truth for what the app can actually do.

architecture.description: The Expo app talks REST and websockets to one TypeScript/Express service. The service keeps users, associations, posts, comments, likes, and reports in PostgreSQL (Sequelize) and conversations and marketplace collections in MongoDB (Mongoose). A BullMQ push queue in Redis feeds a worker that delivers to Expo/FCM and polls for receipts, Socket.IO handles realtime chat, and a Lydia payment module receives webhooks and purchase callbacks.

caseStudy.implementation:
The API is a TypeScript Express service with TypeDI dependency injection: the Lydia provider is bound to a PaymentProvider interface token at boot, so route controllers depend on the interface, not the vendor. A central validationErrorHandler catches express-validator and zod failures, Swagger is generated from the route surface, and the PostgreSQL models are registered explicitly and synced at startup.

The push pipeline is a queue, not a fire-and-forget call. A BullMQ push queue with its own Redis connection feeds a worker (expo-server-sdk) whose concurrency is environment-driven; after every batch the worker polls Expo push receipts on a 60-second interval, and device tokens are registered through dedicated device routes so the app never guesses a token. Firebase Cloud Messaging setup is documented end to end (FCM_SETUP guide, Expo package name, Android registration).

Realtime chat runs on Socket.IO rooms with a Pusher service for presence; the conversational surface also went through a Supabase realtime iteration (SQL functions committed in the app repo) before consolidating in the backend. The mobile app is expo-router with tab groups (home, events, deals, wavezone, profile), auth flows, stories, image picking, QR codes, calendar pickers, i18n, and React Query + Zustand state. Everything orchestrates through Docker Compose — postgres, mongo, redis, API — so the stack runs locally as a unit.

challenges.title: Push delivery is a reliability problem, not a function call
challenges.resolution: Push moved into a BullMQ queue with a dedicated worker, environment-driven concurrency, and 60-second receipt polling so undelivered notifications get reconciled instead of silently lost.

challenges.title: Two data stores under one API
challenges.resolution: PostgreSQL (Sequelize) owns the social core — users, associations, posts, likes, comments, reports — while MongoDB (Mongoose) owns conversations and marketplace collections; services, not controllers, decide which store a request touches.

challenges.title: Payments must be swappable
challenges.resolution: The Lydia provider sits behind a PaymentProvider interface token in TypeDI, with webhook and purchase-callback endpoints describing the contract — controllers never import the vendor.

challenges.title: Chat backend churned before stabilizing
challenges.resolution: An earlier Supabase-realtime iteration (committed SQL functions) was replaced by Socket.IO + Pusher in the backend; the honest cost is that the conversation surface carries two mental models in the repo history.

lessons: Push notifications are a delivery pipeline — queue, worker, receipt reconciliation — and the send call is the smallest part of it.
A payments integration deserves a provider boundary: a DI token let the app change vendors without touching controllers.
Two data stores are fine when each serves a document shape: relational for the social graph, document for messages and listings.
The repos commit no tests. Coverage claims would be lies, so the gap is stated here instead of papered over.
future: Add an automated test suite (unit + integration) and a CI gate before any public release.
Profile the push pipeline and publish delivery-rate metrics instead of assuming they are fine.
Split the API into bounded-context services only if the route surface keeps growing past what one deployable can own.
Validate the Lydia tutoring-purchase path against real production callbacks.
